chunks: My father (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Ahmad ibn Idris narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad, who said: Abu Abdillah al-Razi narrated to us, from al-Hasan ibn al-Husayn, from Yasin al-Darir [A] and others, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father (peace be upon them both), who said:

A man proposed marriage to a group of people, and they asked him: 'What is your trade?' He said: 'I sell animals (dawaab).' So they married him off, but it turned out he was selling donkeys (sananeer), so they disputed [the marriage] and went to Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him), and he validated his marriage, saying: 'Donkeys are animals.'
ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic legal ruling on marriage contracts when the groom's specific trade differs from the general description given?
ai.summary: Recorded in Shaykh al-Saduq’s *Ma'ani al-Akhbar* under 'Rare Meanings,' this hadith illustrates the principle of *istishab* (presumption of continuity) and linguistic generality in Shia jurisprudence. Imam Ali (AS) validated the marriage by ruling that 'donkeys' (*sananeer*) are subsumed under the general term 'animals' (*dawaab*), demonstrating that unless a specific exclusion is stated, the broader category governs the contract. This case highlights the scholarly emphasis on contextual interpretation of trade professions in marital agreements.
